::: {.why}
The relationship you noticed last night is the Black-Scholes PDE rearranged, which means it is exact rather than approximate, and stating it that way is how the trade-off gets explained in an interview.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Derive the gamma-theta relationship from the PDE and state it for a zero-rate case in one line.
- Say what being long gamma in a quiet market costs you per day, in dollars, for a specific position.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Rearrange the PDE: with rates at zero, theta equals minus half the variance times the square of the spot times gamma. That single line says that time decay is exactly the cost of the convexity you own, priced at the implied variance. Verify it numerically against your greeks across a grid.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Make it concrete in money: for a specific long straddle on a specific underlying, compute the daily theta in dollars and the move in the underlying that would break even against it. That break-even move is the implied daily volatility, which is a fact worth having in your hands rather than in a formula.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Then reverse it: for a short position, state the daily income and the move that wipes it out, and note the asymmetry between the two cases.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
The gamma-theta identity verified numerically, plus a dollar break-even move computed for a specific straddle.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Gamma and theta have opposite signs for a reason. State it, and say what it implies for a long-gamma position in a quiet market.
:::
